title: Kaliya's Wives Plead for His Life
story:
In a deep pool of the Yamuna, the serpent king Kaliya lay still, his many heads drooping and torn where Krishna's feet had come down on them. Krishna, the cowherd boy of Vrindavan who had leapt into the pool to make the river safe again, stood over him, and for a long moment it seemed even the river held its breath. Kaliya, whose poison had made the Yamuna unfit to drink, was broken at last.

Then, from the far side of the water, his wives came forward. Their hair hung loose and their garments had slipped from their shoulders, and they carried their little children in their arms as they waded through the mud. They set the children down before them, lowered themselves to the ground, and laid their bodies before Krishna, hands folded. They did not ask to be spared themselves. They asked that their husband be.

“The punishment is just,” they said. “Our husband is an offender, and your coming into the world is to subdue the wicked. Yet you look with equal eyes even upon the children of your own enemies, and what you give as punishment comes back to us as grace.” Even the blow that had fallen on the proud serpent, they said, was itself a blessing, for it was washing the stain from him.

Then their praise rose through the evening air like the smoke of an offering. They called Krishna by the oldest names they knew: the great Soul, the storehouse of knowledge and wisdom, the one of unbroken power; Time itself, the navel of time, the witness who watches over every part of it; the Self who stands behind the elements and the senses, the breath, the mind and the heart. Homage, they said, to the subtle one who never changes, the seer from whom every scripture flows. Homage to Krishna, to Rama, to the son of Vasudeva. He is the lamp that lights the strands of the world and the one who draws them back into darkness; his play lies beyond all that is made, and yet through him everything made comes to be. He himself desires nothing, and still all the powers of action and of time are held in him. He knows the highest and the lowest, and over all of it he keeps watch.

All the beings of the three worlds — the peaceful, the restless, the bewildered — are only his forms, they told him. But it is the peaceful who are dear to him, and it was to guard them and to hold up what is right that he had come at all.

Then their voices dropped, and they came to the heart of it. “A wrong done once by a husband,” they said, “should be borne with, as one bears with the wrongs of one's own children.” They looked at the great serpent lying still, and then at the boy who had brought him low. “Grant us your favour, Lord. The serpent is giving up his life. Tell us, your servants, what we are to do.”

They had not come to argue that Kaliya was innocent, nor with anger or threats or bargaining. They had come with their children, their loosened hair and their folded hands, and they had laid between the boy and the dying king of serpents the one thing no one had offered Kaliya before: a word spoken on his behalf.

Krishna listened.
reflection: The wives never argue Kaliya's innocence. They accept the punishment as just, then turn that acceptance into their plea — the blow itself, they say, is grace. Their intercession works because it asks for nothing on the serpent's merits, only on Krishna's own evenness of eye.
content_note: Kaliya is shown beaten and near death after Krishna's dance on his heads.
next_story_tease: But the serpent's life still hung upon Krishna's answer.
hero_scene: The wives of Kaliya kneeling before Krishna on the riverbank at dusk, their hair loose and their garments slipping, hands folded, little children pressed close, as the great serpent lies broken in the water behind them.
visual_elements: the broken serpent in the pool
